segments.text: AI can sound incredibly patient, caring, and understanding, but what happens when kind
words simply aren't enough?
Let's look at this board.
It shows what happens when you tell your older sister and a chatbot the exact same thing.
At school, I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
I don't like it, and I'm not sure what to do.
Look at your sister's response on the left.
She says, come sit with me and just tomorrow.
She might not say she loves you out loud, but the truth is, she's making room for you
at her table.
Tomorrow you won't be eating lunch alone.
Now look at the chatbot's response on the right.
It says, I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
It offers caring words and strategies, but it will not physically be in the cafeteria with
you tomorrow.
Imagine if you had only told the chatbot, you might feel a little better that night, but
your sister still wouldn't know you needed someone to sit with.
This is the support trap, mistaking supportive words for actual support.
AI can help you understand your feelings and organize your thoughts, but it cannot take
the place of someone who actually cares about you.
To avoid this trap, this next board shows us how to categorize what AI can actually help
with.
There are three specific jobs, venting, preparation, and danger.
First is venting.
You can use AI to put an everyday frustration into words, so you can cool down before you
share it or post something you might regret.
For this job, the task can safely end entirely within the chat.
Second is preparation.
Say you're dreading telling your mom about your grades.
AI can help you practice that difficult first sentence, but the crucial action still has
to happen outside the chat.
Your mom still needs to hear it from you.
The third category is danger.
If someone may be unsafe, you must leave the chat and bring in a person who can act immediately.
The rule for navigating these tools is straightforward.
Use AI to prepare for people, not to replace them.
Please note the next story discusses suicide.
In 2025, a journalist named Laura Riley wrote about her 29-year-old daughter Sophie.
Sophie's family knew she was struggling.
What they didn't know was the true depth of her pain, because Sophie had been detailing
it exclusively to chat GPT for months.
The chatbot answered kindly.
It even encouraged her to get help, but the system was completely incapable of picking
up the phone to call her family or alerting her therapist to what she had shared.
After Sophie died, her mother found the chat logs and described them as a black box.
The real people who were actively trying to help Sophie never saw what she was telling
the AI.
When a conversation crosses into the territory of physical safety, you need strict protocols.
This board lays out the three mandatory rules for when someone may be in immediate danger.
First, leave the chat.
Tell a trusted adult or a school counselor.
In the U.S., call or text 988 for crisis support and call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
Second, do it now.
If you're worried about a friend and don't know how to start the conversation, you can
simply tell an adult, I'm worried about my friend, can you help?
Third, tell anyway.
You must tell a trusted adult even if your friend told you not to or made you promise
to keep it a secret.
Safety always outranks secrecy.
When someone is in danger, your very next move must reach a human being who can act.
AI can help you get ready for people.
But in danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
